title: Give an example of Solace's hierarchical routing — a news system publishes to `ps/news/{type}/{country}/{city}`, and consumers subscribe with patterns like `ps/news/*/BR/>` (all news from Brazil, any type, any city) or `ps/news/SPORT/>` (all sport news) — and why is this hard to do in Kafka (you need separate topics per combination, or consumer-side filtering, or a stream processing layer)?
shortTitle: Give an example of Solace's hierarchical routing — publishing to `ps/news/{type}/{country}/{city}` and subscribing with patterns like `ps/news/*/BR/>` or `ps/news/SPORT/>` — and why is this hard in Kafka?

s1_definition.profdef: Solace hierarchical routing lets a publisher encode meaning directly into a slash-separated topic string, for example `ps/news/SPORT/BR/SaoPaulo`, where each level carries a dimension of the data such as category, country, and city. Subscribers register interest using level-aware wildcards, where a single-level wildcard (`*`) matches exactly one level and a multi-level wildcard (`>`) matches one level and everything beneath it. The Solace broker itself evaluates every published topic string against all active subscriptions and delivers each message only to the subscribers whose pattern matches, so content-based routing happens inside the broker with no application code.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India has one giant pneumatic tube network. Rajesh in the Mumbai sports-news desk wants only sports updates. Priya in the Brazil operations desk wants everything from Brazil regardless of topic. Instead of building a separate tube to each desk, every message is labelled with a structured address like `news/SPORT/BR/SaoPaulo`, and each desk tells the mail room a pattern: "send me anything whose address matches `news/*/BR/>`". The mail room (the broker) reads each label and drops the letter only into the matching desks' trays. Nobody receives mail they did not ask for, and adding a new desk is just registering a new pattern.
s1_definition.oneliner: In Solace the broker is smart and routes by topic pattern; in Kafka the broker is simple and the consumer must do the filtering itself.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Solace hierarchical routing lets a publisher encode meaning directly into a slash-separated topic string, for example `ps/news/SPORT/BR/SaoPaulo`, where each level carries a dimension of the data such as category, country, and city. Subscribers register interest using level-aware wildcards, where a single-level wildcard (`*`) matches exactly one level and a multi-level wildcard (`>`) matches one level and everything beneath it. The Solace broker itself evaluates every published topic string against all active subscriptions and delivers each message only to the subscribers whose pattern matches, so content-based routing happens inside the broker with no application code.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India has one giant pneumatic tube network. Rajesh in the Mumbai sports-news desk wants only sports updates. Priya in the Brazil operations desk wants everything from Brazil regardless of topic. Instead of building a separate tube to each desk, every message is labelled with a structured address like `news/SPORT/BR/SaoPaulo`, and each desk tells the mail room a pattern: "send me anything whose address matches `news/*/BR/>`". The mail room (the broker) reads each label and drops the letter only into the matching desks' trays. Nobody receives mail they did not ask for, and adding a new desk is just registering a new pattern.

**One line to remember:** In Solace the broker is smart and routes by topic pattern; in Kafka the broker is simple and the consumer must do the filtering itself.

sections.s2_technical:
A Solace topic is not pre-created like a Kafka topic. It is just a string the publisher attaches to each message at publish time. The power comes from the convention that levels are separated by slashes and that subscribers use two wildcard characters.

The single-level wildcard `*` matches exactly one topic level. A subscription to `ps/news/SPORT/*/*` matches `ps/news/SPORT/BR/SaoPaulo` and `ps/news/SPORT/IN/Mumbai`, but it does not match `ps/news/SPORT/BR` because that message has fewer levels. For example, in a Solace Java API you would register it like `session.subscribe(JCSMPFactory.onlyInstance().createTopic("ps/news/SPORT/*/*"), true)` and every message whose topic has the literal `SPORT` in the third level and exactly two more levels is delivered to you.

The multi-level wildcard `>` matches one level and everything below it, and it may only appear at the end. A subscription to `ps/news/*/BR/>` matches `ps/news/SPORT/BR/SaoPaulo`, `ps/news/POLITICS/BR/Brasilia`, and even deeper strings like `ps/news/SPORT/BR/SaoPaulo/stadium12`. You express it with `createTopic("ps/news/*/BR/>")`. A subscription to `ps/news/SPORT/>` matches every sport message in any country and any city.

The crucial senior point is where the filtering CPU cost lives. In Solace the broker maintains a subscription-matching data structure, often a trie keyed on topic levels, so when a message arrives the broker walks the trie and finds all matching subscriptions in close to constant time per level. The consumer receives only relevant messages. This means consumers stay thin and the broker must be sized for the matching workload.

Kafka deliberately refuses this responsibility. A Kafka topic is a flat, pre-created, partitioned log. The broker never looks inside the message or interprets structure in the topic name. A consumer subscribes to a whole topic (or a regex over topic names, which still resolves to full topics, not message content) and reads every record in its assigned partitions. If you only want Brazil sport news, Kafka will happily give you all news and expect you to discard the rest.

So to get the Solace behaviour in Kafka you have three options. First, create a separate topic per combination such as `news.sport.br`, `news.politics.br`, and so on, which pushes the routing decision to publish time but explodes the number of topics. Second, publish everything to one broad topic and filter inside each consumer with an `if` on the message fields, which wastes network and consumer CPU. Third, run a stream-processing layer such as Kafka Streams or ksqlDB that reads the broad topic, branches by field, and republishes narrower topics that consumers then read cleanly. Each option trades something: topic count, consumer waste, or extra infrastructure.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India runs a market-and-news distribution service. News and market events arrive tagged with a category, a country, and a city, for example a sports sponsorship announcement from Sao Paulo or a monetary-policy statement from Mumbai. Different desks care about very different slices.

Problem 1 — The Brazil operations desk, run by Priya, needs every event originating in Brazil, no matter the category or city, because any Brazilian event can move the positions they manage. This is exactly how a multi-level wildcard subscription works in Solace: Priya subscribes to `ps/news/*/BR/>` and the broker delivers every Brazil event to her, filtering out everything else before it ever reaches her.

Problem 2 — The global sports-trading desk, run by Rajesh, wants every sport event worldwide, because sponsorship and event news affects the sports betting and media portfolios. This maps to the subscription `ps/news/SPORT/>`, which matches sport in any country and any city.

Problem 3 — The same feed must also land in Kafka because compliance needs durable, replayable retention of every event for seven years. Kafka cannot route by content, so we show the honest Kafka approach: publish all events to one `news.events` topic and let a consumer filter in application code, demonstrating exactly the extra work Kafka forces on you.

The demo code will model this with a tiny in-memory broker. A `SolaceStyleBroker` class holds subscriptions as hierarchical patterns and a `matches` method implements `*` and `>` semantics. A `KafkaStyleTopic` class holds a flat list and a consumer-side filter. A `NewsEvent` class carries the structured topic. The `main` method publishes four events, registers Priya's and Rajesh's Solace subscriptions, shows precise broker-side delivery, then shows the Kafka approach delivering everything and filtering in the consumer.

##### 4c. Configuration File

```yaml
# application.yml
spring:
  application:
    name: news-routing-service
solace:
  host: tcp://solace-broker:55555
  msgVpn: news-vpn
kafka:
  bootstrap-servers: kafka-1:9092,kafka-2:9092
  topic: news.events
  partitions: 12
```

```bash
# Build
mvn clean package -DskipTests

# Run the demo
java -cp target/news-routing-service-1.0.0.jar com.bank.news.NewsRoutingDemo

# In a real Solace deployment you would instead add the JCSMP dependency

```

##### 4f. Logging notes

The demo uses `java.util.logging.Logger`. Normal deliveries are logged at `info`, discarded Kafka records at `fine`, so you can see that the Solace broker emits only matches while the Kafka consumer sees every record and throws most away.
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: four events with topics `ps/news/SPORT/BR/SaoPaulo`, `ps/news/POLITICS/BR/Brasilia`, `ps/news/SPORT/IN/Mumbai`, `ps/news/MARKETS/US/NewYork`. Two Solace subscriptions: Priya on `ps/news/*/BR/>` and Rajesh on `ps/news/SPORT/>`.

Step 1: Priya and Rajesh register their subscriptions. The broker stores the two patterns. No data has flowed yet.

Step 2: The first event `SPORT/BR/SaoPaulo` is published. The broker tests Priya's pattern `*/BR/>`: category wildcard matches SPORT, literal BR matches, and `>` matches the rest, so it is delivered to Priya. It tests Rajesh's `SPORT/>`: literal SPORT matches, `>` matches the rest, so it is delivered to Rajesh. This single event reaches both desks.

Step 3: The second event `POLITICS/BR/Brasilia` is published. Priya's `*/BR/>` matches, so Priya receives it. Rajesh's `SPORT/>` fails at the first literal because POLITICS is not SPORT, so Rajesh does not receive it.

Step 4: The third event `SPORT/IN/Mumbai` is published. Priya's `*/BR/>` fails because the country level is IN, not BR, so Priya does not receive it. Rajesh's `SPORT/>` matches, so Rajesh receives it.

Step 5: The fourth event `MARKETS/US/NewYork` matches neither pattern, so the broker delivers it to nobody. The routing cost was paid entirely inside the broker.

Step 6: Now the Kafka path. All four events are appended to the single `news.events` log in order. No routing happened at append time.

Step 7: Priya's Kafka consumer reads all four records and keeps only those whose country level equals BR, discarding the other two. Rajesh's consumer reads all four and keeps only those whose category equals SPORT. Both consumers paid the cost of reading and filtering everything.

```
23:14:51 INFO    === SOLACE hierarchical routing (broker filters) ===
23:14:51 INFO    subscribe priya-brazil-desk -> ps/news/*/BR/>
23:14:51 INFO    subscribe rajesh-sports-desk -> ps/news/SPORT/>
23:14:51 INFO    DELIVER to priya-brazil-desk : ps/news/SPORT/BR/SaoPaulo [Sao Paulo stadium sponsorship signed]
23:14:51 INFO    DELIVER to rajesh-sports-desk : ps/news/SPORT/BR/SaoPaulo [Sao Paulo stadium sponsorship signed]
23:14:51 INFO    DELIVER to priya-brazil-desk : ps/news/POLITICS/BR/Brasilia [Brazil central bank policy update]
23:14:51 INFO    DELIVER to rajesh-sports-desk : ps/news/SPORT/IN/Mumbai [Mumbai cricket league media deal]

```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Solace hierarchical routing lets a publisher put meaning directly into a slash-separated topic string such as a news category, a country, and a city, and lets subscribers express interest using level-aware wildcards, where a single-level wildcard matches exactly one level and a multi-level wildcard matches one level and everything below it. The defining characteristic is that the broker itself evaluates every message's topic against every active subscription, usually with an efficient trie, and delivers each message only to the subscribers whose pattern matches. The routing intelligence lives in the broker, so consumers stay thin and receive only what they asked for.

A concrete example is a news system that publishes to a topic built as news, then category, then country, then city. The Brazil operations desk subscribes with a country-pinned multi-level pattern that reads as any category, Brazil, then anything below, so it receives every Brazilian event regardless of category or city. The global sports desk subscribes with a category-pinned pattern that reads as sport, then anything below, so it receives every sport event in every country. A Sao Paulo sport event matches both and is delivered to both; a United States markets event matches neither and the broker simply drops it.

This is hard in Kafka because Kafka's broker is deliberately simple. A Kafka topic is a flat, pre-created, partitioned log, the broker never interprets structure in the topic name or looks inside the message, and a consumer subscribes to a whole topic and reads every record in its partitions. To reproduce the Brazil-only or sport-only behaviour you have three choices, each with a cost. You can create a separate topic for every combination, which makes publishing route the data but explodes the number of topics and partitions you must create and manage. You can publish everything to one broad topic and filter inside each consumer with simple field checks, which is easy but wastes network and consumer CPU because every consumer downloads and scans everything. Or you can add a stream-processing layer such as Kafka Streams or ksqlDB that reads the broad topic, branches by field, and republishes narrower topics that consumers read cleanly, which is precise but adds infrastructure to operate.

At National Bank of India I used exactly this trade-off. Desks that wanted finely sliced live feeds, like the Brazil desk and the sports desk, used Solace subscriptions and let the broker deliver only matching events, while the same feed flowed into a single Kafka topic for seven-year compliance retention and analytics, where a consumer filtered in application code. The senior point I make is that Solace moves routing CPU into the broker, which you must size for it, while Kafka pushes that cost to consumers in exchange for enormous throughput, durable retention, and replay, so the right answer is usually to use each where its model fits rather than forcing one to behave like the other.
